title: Version 1.6.122
notes: A workflow that saves a document named at run time now tells you the real name it used, instead of showing the placeholder.

title: Builds stop testing themselves twice
notes: Building a workflow is much faster — Atlas no longer runs the whole workflow during the build and then again when you press Run test. Proving it works is what the test is for.
A workflow that saves into a document named at run time is no longer told it delivered nowhere.

title: Version 1.6.120
notes: A workflow you published earlier no longer shows its approval screen when you come back to it — it opens on its dashboard, where it belongs.

title: Going live, and a test you can watch
notes: Publishing a workflow now takes you straight to its dashboard — the approval screen no longer stays up after you've approved it.
A workflow that saves into a Google Doc titled with the date can now pass its own test instead of being told it delivered nowhere.
While a test runs, the panel shows how many of your examples have run so far.
The screens before Run test name your destination in plain words instead of showing an internal code name.

title: The build tells you what it's doing while it tests
notes: And a workflow is no longer rebuilt because the AI ran out of time — that's not a fault in your workflow.

title: A correct workflow is no longer told it delivers nowhere
notes: Atlas recognised Airtable's identifiers but not Google's, so a Sheets workflow was accused of dropping everything it wrote.

title: The build stops asking what you already told it
notes: Name a spreadsheet you own and Atlas just uses it; name one you don't and it creates it. No question mid-build.

title: Create a spreadsheet you don't have yet
notes: Asked for a sheet that doesn't exist, Atlas now offers to create it instead of listing ten you didn't ask for.

title: Clearer wording on the cards you read before going live
notes: Email filters read as plain English, the step card names the sheet it writes to, and a brand-new account no longer opens on a list of release notes.

title: A calendar booking is checked against your calendar, not the event's name
notes: Atlas no longer treats an event's title as the place it was saved, so a correctly booked demo is no longer reported as a broken promise.

title: Fewer rebuilds — Atlas stops re-checking things it already did
notes: The build reviewer no longer orders a rebuild for something the workflow already contains, or for a tool that doesn't exist.

title: The spreadsheet picker only appears when you're writing to a spreadsheet
notes: A workflow that reads email and posts to Slack no longer stops to ask which Google Sheet to write to.

title: Atlas won't design a workflow it can't build
notes: On a workspace with nothing connected, Atlas now leads with what to connect instead of designing the workflow first and mentioning the problem at the end.

title: Slack events now reach every workspace that connected them
notes: If the same Slack workspace is connected by more than one Atlas workspace, events and approval clicks now reach all of them instead of whichever one was found first.

title: A Slack-triggered workflow can no longer go live if Slack can't reach Atlas
notes: Atlas now refuses to publish a workflow that starts from Slack when Slack has never delivered an event — instead of showing it as live while nothing happens.

title: Atlas says what needs connecting before it designs with it
notes: On a new workspace, Atlas now tells you which apps to connect instead of asking which Slack channel to use and calling an inbox you haven't connected 'your connected inbox'.

title: Give Atlas a test case without it rebuilding your workflow
notes: Every path in a workflow now gets its own test input, and describing a case yourself adds it instead of rebuilding the whole thing.

title: A workflow that only acts on one path can go live
notes: A workflow that classifies first — act on a match, stay quiet otherwise — no longer fails its own check when a real, unrelated email comes through.

title: Pick your spreadsheet, don't paste its ID
notes: Atlas now reads your Google Sheets and offers them by name, the way it already did for Airtable — instead of asking you to dig an ID out of a URL.

title: Atlas won't ask you for things it should look up
notes: Atlas no longer asks for internal identifiers like a spreadsheet ID, no longer asks the same thing twice, and limits itself to three questions per build — deciding the rest so you can correct it on the plan.

title: Atlas knows where an inbox message actually goes
notes: Deliveries to your Atlas inbox were internally recorded as going to the message's own subject line. They now correctly record the inbox itself.

title: Workflows can now use your Knowledge documents
notes: A workflow can search your uploaded documents while it runs, and save new material back to them. Atlas also now tells you plainly when your Knowledge is empty instead of agreeing that it can use it.

title: Atlas can see everything your connected apps can do
notes: Airtable's and the web connector's abilities were invisible to the AI while building — three connected services were being described as able to do nothing. The list now comes from the same place the app itself uses.

title: Atlas now knows what its own triggers are called
notes: The list of ways a workflow can be started was being sent to the AI as numbers instead of names. It now comes from the one place that defines which triggers actually work.

title: Atlas no longer offers ways to start a workflow that don't work
notes: Two kinds of trigger — a webhook URL and a run-once trigger — were being offered in conversation but could never actually be published. Asking to 'run this once' now sets up a manual trigger, which does the same thing and works.

title: Fewer false alarms in Atlas's self-check
notes: The self-check no longer reports a contradiction when a workflow has several promises and its summary mentions only one of them.

title: Fewer false alarms in Atlas's self-check
notes: The check that looks for a workflow contradicting itself no longer flags the channel a workflow listens to as a missing destination.

title: A workflow with nothing to do is no longer marked failed
notes: When a workflow processes each item in a list and the list is empty, that now reads as 'nothing to prove either way' instead of a broken promise.

title: Destinations travel with the workflow
notes: The list of places a workflow writes now stays attached to it when it is published, not just the references to them.

title: Where a workflow writes is now settled once
notes: The place a workflow sends or writes to is recorded once and referred to by both the workflow's promise and the step that does the work, so the two can no longer drift apart.

title: Atlas checks its own work before showing it to you
notes: Every finished build is now checked for places where it contradicts itself — for example a promise that names one destination while the step it built names another. Findings are recorded, not acted on.

title: Connectors decide their own behaviour
notes: Each connector's own description of what it does — and where it writes — is now what Atlas actually reads. A hardcoded internal list had been silently overriding it for six of them.

title: Calendar workflows stop failing their own check
notes: A workflow that books a calendar event no longer reports that nothing reached your calendar. Promises written as "Google Calendar" were being checked against Gmail.

title: The promise follows the answer you gave
notes: When Atlas asks where something should go, your answer now updates the workflow's promise as well as the step. Before, the promise kept Atlas's first guess at the destination, which made correct workflows fail their own check and rebuild several times.

title: A build you look away from is no longer lost
notes: If you open another workflow while Atlas is building, the finished build is now waiting for you when you come back instead of disappearing. Atlas also no longer mixes up your Slack account with your email address when you ask it to send something to you.

title: The agreement sweep: 262 combinations, zero disagreements
notes: The declaration audit asks whether everything is declared; it could not have caught two consumers of the same table asking the question differently. This sweeps every write capability by every connector spelling by both node forms, plus every promise against every other delivery, and asserts build-time and runtime agree. Registry-driven, so tomorrow's connector is swept tomorrow.

title: Build-time and runtime disagreed about where a Google Doc lives
notes: A digest written to a Google Doc satisfied its promise at build time and failed it at run time: build-time consults the connector alias table, runtime compared two canonical scalars, docs vs drive. Writing the same promise as 'docs:' passed both. Both halves now read the same table, directed rather than symmetric.

title: The declaration audit: 19 of 28 capabilities were guesses
notes: Asked the whole question at once instead of one build at a time. 19 of 28 capabilities declared no effect, so a verb regex decided; three were writes seen as reads, including airtable_delete_record — the most destructive capability shipped — which escaped both the duplicate-protection and approval-strength guards. No build had ever exercised it because nothing promises a deletion.

title: A connected connector reported as not connected
notes: Atlas designed a Google Doc digest over three turns, took the approval, then refused to build because 'gdrive is not connected' — Google Workspace was connected. CONNECTOR_ALIASES spelled out gdocs and gcal but not gdrive or gsheets. Fixed as a family: a vendor prefix run together with the service name.

title: No templates on the last card before a real send
notes: The approval card's question printed raw {{templates}} directly above the row fixed for that hours earlier, the trigger filter showed query syntax, and every event trigger was described as a Slack message — false for an Airtable record change. The reference rule now lives in one place shared by both rows.

title: Add a column to a table you named, not just one you identified
notes: The Airtable schema endpoint accepts only the tbl-id, while every other capability here and every person uses the table name — so a retry carrying 'Companies' got NOT_FOUND. Resolved from the schema read the idempotency check already does, and the failure is said in words.

title: The confirm button went dead after a reload
notes: Action-card ids came from a counter that restarts on every mount, so a card minted after a reload collided with a finished card restored from before it. The click handler looked up by id, found the old one, saw it had already run, and returned — silently, with no way to recover.

title: Atlas could only ever make one kind of Airtable column
notes: It offered to add an 'Intro Email Sent' checkbox, was confirmed, and failed: most Airtable field types need required options and the connector sent none, so only the singleLineText default ever worked. Defaults now supplied per type, select columns refused in words rather than guessed, and the raw API sentence no longer reaches the chat card.

title: The person building it has the last word
notes: Three ways Atlas contradicted something the user had just said: the sufficiency critic ordered a rebuild arguing against an explicit instruction, the promise text kept describing the pre-revision behaviour, and the approval card never showed the approver what they would be shown. None corrupted a spec; each made Atlas say something untrue of the workflow it had built.

title: A login email is not a Slack account
notes: Two approval builds addressed their Slack DM to the operator's Atlas login, which has no Slack account, so every run failed 'no Slack user matches' and neither could verify. The DM target is now resolved from the connected workspace, and an unmatched login is never guessed at — Atlas asks instead, because DMing the nearest match would deliver private drafts to a colleague. users.list is also paginated now.

title: The plan you revised is the plan that gets built
notes: The previous fix read '/with a change/' out of a diagnostic string and missed the path a person actually takes: revising the plan in chat re-renders it, and the approval that follows carries no modification, so the revision was invisible and the rejected trigger filter survived again. The route now declares it, from planRounds.

title: A quiet path is not a broken promise
notes: Two fixes from a pricing-approval build. Examples labelled 'should not trigger workflow' were scored as broken promises for sending nothing — evaluation order meant a negative never reached the branch written for it, and only the safer in-flow-classifier design failed. And a trigger the user asked to change could not be changed: derived once, then pinned both by the spec merge and by the generate prompt, so the approved plan and the built workflow disagreed.

title: A promise that names the product names no address
notes: Three consecutive prod builds of one correct workflow phrased the same promise three ways — tasks:My Tasks, google_tasks:My Tasks, tasks:Google Tasks — and each needed its own fix. The third names no destination: 'a task in Google Tasks' is the connector said twice. A locator that only repeats the product is now treated as no address, the same judgement already made for templates, opaque provider ids and the inbox.

title: Google Tasks was missing from the connector vocabulary
notes: canonicalConnector('google_tasks') resolved to GMAIL — there was no tasks entry in the alias table, so the fallback matched 'google', which appears first in Gmail's aliases. And satisfiesAssertion compared the connector raw while the runtime check had always canonicalised, so the two halves of one question disagreed. A promise about a task list could not be kept by the step that kept it.

title: Keep the sub-service name when a write is declared
notes: Declaring effect: write routed Google capabilities through declaredWriteEffect, which took the connector from the capability ('google') instead of the id ('tasks') — so a promise written as 'tasks:My Tasks' failed on the connector even though the destination was now correct. Both names are kept. Caught by re-running the real build on prod; the third decider had no test.

title: Declare where a write lands; one gate on rebuilds
notes: A correct workflow was told it delivered nowhere: tasks_create's destination was guessed from key names, so the task's own title was reported as the place it was written. Capabilities now declare locatorKeys. And the same false fact bought three Opus rebuilds from three different routes — replaced three per-route guards with one gate at generate, keyed on the promise a complaint concerns.

title: You can see what you're approving, and the conversation carries on
notes: When Atlas asks you to confirm actions like adding columns, each row now names the column and the table instead of repeating the capability's name. And once they've run, Atlas picks the conversation back up instead of stopping.

title: A workflow no longer sets itself up on every run
notes: When Atlas offers to add a column or create a channel for you, that now happens once while the workflow is being built — not on every single run. Previously those steps landed inside the workflow, where the second run would fail on them and stop before doing anything.

title: Scheduled workflows run at the time you asked for
notes: A schedule built without an explicit timezone was being stored with none at all, so it ran in the server's zone — a workflow you were told runs at 5pm Chicago would have fired at noon. New schedules now carry your timezone. Also: Atlas stops rebuilding a workflow when the same objection comes back in different words, and search steps show what they look for rather than their query syntax.

title: Atlas knows how to build per-item work
notes: Asking Atlas to go through each of something and act on some of them — sort each email, flag each overdue row — used to send it round in circles: it knew loops can't contain routing, concluded per-item work was impossible, and judged the whole batch instead. It now knows the shape that works.

title: The workflow diagram sits under the figures
notes: On a workflow's overview the diagram now sits below Time saved / Last run / Baseline and above the baseline setup, so the numbers you came for lead the page.

title: Going live takes you to the dashboard
notes: Publishing now opens the workflow's dashboard directly, and reopening Atlas takes you there too. The "Workflow is live" card in between is gone — it only had a button to the dashboard on it, and it came back every time you opened the app.

title: Drag the workflow diagram with either mouse button
notes: Left-click and drag now pans the diagram, as well as the scroll wheel.

title: Pan and zoom the workflow diagram
notes: The diagram now sits on the same dotted canvas as the builder. Hold the scroll wheel and move the mouse to pan; scroll to zoom in and out around the pointer. Double-click to put it back where it started.

title: The workflow diagram takes less of the page
notes: It sat in the fixed header, so it owned the top of every workflow page and no amount of scrolling got past it. It now sits at the top of the overview and scrolls away, capped shorter, and centred.

title: The workflow page draws the real workflow
notes: Opening a workflow now shows the actual diagram — branches, approval gates and all — instead of a flat row of names that could not show a branch at all. It is the same picture the builder draws. Approval steps also stop listing "Timeout" as something a person can answer; a timeout is what happens when nobody does, and that is stated on the next line.

title: The procedure document states an approval's deadline
notes: The document listed what a person can answer at an approval step but not what happens if nobody does — it read a different config shape than the approval card, so on real workflows the deadline was silently missing.

title: The workflow page reads in plain English too
notes: The step strip and status chip on the workflow page were the last two places still showing machine text — EXTRACT, BRANCH, HUMAN, a lambda symbol, and "Gmail: is:unread". They now match the rest of the product.

title: The go-live screen and the live workflow header, in plain English
notes: The screen before Go live and the live workflow page had a fourth set of step labels of their own — BRANCH, HUMAN, AI STEP — and squeezed a 12-step workflow into columns about 50px wide, so the headings ran into each other. They now use the same words as everywhere else, wrap onto several rows, and the trigger reads "A new email arrives · unread" instead of "is:unread".

title: Plain English on every screen, and the workflow page reorganised
notes: Steps now say what they do — "Asks a person", "Picks a path", "Sends it" — instead of LLM PROMPT, BRANCH and CONNECTOR-ACTION, and they say the same thing on the builder, the workflow page and the procedure document. Gmail filters read as "emails that are unread". The procedure document now lists where each route goes and what an approval's timeout means, and no longer prints node ids or the AI's raw prompt. Opening a workflow lands on its overview, with run history underneath the baseline.

title: The flow diagram stays put while you approve steps
notes: Approving a step with a long description was impossible: the page kept scrolling itself back down, taking the flow diagram — and the tick you approve with — off screen. The conversation now only follows the bottom if you are already there.

title: Approving the last step releases the test
notes: If the connection dropped mid-build, approving your final step used to leave the page stuck on "Building…" with Run test greyed out. It now unlocks the test panel instead of waiting for a reply that could never arrive. Scheduled workflows also show their timezone, so you never see a bare "8:00 AM".

title: The step count matches the steps you approve
notes: The workflow panel counted the steps without the trigger, so it could read 3 steps beside an approval queue asking you to confirm 4.

title: Plainer English, your own clock, and honest offers
notes: Times and schedules now use your own timezone instead of UTC, and Atlas confirms both the exact time and how often a workflow runs before building it.
Atlas can no longer offer to produce something the workflow will not actually make — an offer that mentioned a document the build never created is now caught and rewritten.
Step cards, test results and the workflow panel are plain English throughout: no identifiers, no JSON, no template code, and the step count now matches the steps you approve.
A workflow you had approved every step of could get stuck permanently untestable after a deploy, with Run test greyed out and no error shown. Fixed.

title: The approval message now counts as proof
notes: When a workflow asks you to approve something on Slack, that message is now counted as one of the promises it kept. It was being sent but not checked, so a workflow could go live with Atlas saying that part was 'still unproven' — on a run that had actually sent it.

title: Approval workflows can pass their own test
notes: A workflow with an approval step could never pass its own test. Atlas tries each approval both ways — approving and rejecting — but it was checking the 'post it' promise against the wrong decision, so every reject run was counted as a broken promise for not posting the thing that rejecting exists to withhold. Go live stayed locked on workflows that were behaving exactly as designed.

title: Faster builds, and Airtable workflows can pass their test
notes: Building a workflow no longer rebuilds itself several times over. A build that was already correct could be sent back up to four times — around ten minutes — because a second check disagreed with one that had already passed. Builds should now finish in a single pass, and the extra time no longer eats into generating a test example for each path.

A workflow that writes to Airtable can now pass its own test. A record that was created successfully was reported as never delivered, which kept Go live locked on a workflow that had done exactly what it promised.

title: Scheduled workflows run at the right hour
notes: A workflow set to run at 9am was firing at 4am — the schedule ignored the timezone you chose and used the server's. It now runs at the hour you asked for, in the timezone you asked for.

title: Times are now local, not UTC
notes: Atlas now tells the time in your timezone rather than UTC — and because UTC rolls over to tomorrow in the evening, this also makes "today" correct after about 7pm Central.

title: Atlas knows what day it is
notes: Fixes the date in chat. Atlas now reads the real date on every path — chatting, building a workflow, and running one.

title: Atlas knows what day it is
notes: Atlas now knows the current date everywhere — in chat, while building a workflow, and while running one. It previously answered from memory and could be a year out.

title: Correct dates, and safer go-live
notes: Workflows now know today's date. A step that wrote "today" could previously produce a date over a year out, and the test would still report the promise kept — that is fixed for both building and running.
Resuming a paused workflow now re-arms its trigger, and a workflow that has never been published can no longer be switched live from the console.
A step that changes something in another system is now recognised from what the connector declares rather than from its name, so approval prompts and duplicate protection fire on every write.

title: Safer, smarter testing
notes: Running a test never sends real messages now, and it confirms each destination actually exists before it says a step will deliver. Workflows with an approval step test themselves — both the approve and the reject path — with no clicking.

title: The sign-in screen no longer offers account creation
notes: Atlas is a product you don't buy yourself. 'Create an account' is now removed from the sign-in screen for good — it can't reappear on its own.

title: A 'should not happen' test case can't be marked as passed
notes: A generated test case meaning 'this should NOT trigger' was being shown with a green tick as if the workflow had proven it stays quiet — while it had actually run and delivered. It's now correctly shown as 'not checked'.

title: A forgotten connection is fixed in seconds, not minutes
notes: When Atlas built a delivery step but forgot to connect it, it used to rebuild the whole workflow to fix it. It now just adds the one missing connection — the slow rebuild is gone for that case.

title: Workflows get their name up front
notes: Atlas now names a workflow when you approve its plan, instead of leaving it to the final build step — which occasionally forgot, forcing a slow rebuild just to add a title.

title: Builds fix small mistakes instead of starting over
notes: When Atlas made a small error building a workflow — a missing name, an unwired step — it used to rebuild the entire workflow from scratch, several times, costing minutes. It now fixes the small thing and moves on.

title: Smaller fixes to questions, buttons, and diagnostics
notes: Only the newest question keeps its quick-answer buttons; a build paused when you refresh now explains how to continue; and internal build logs now record which workspace a build belongs to.

title: A workflow with several paths now tests all of them
notes: Atlas used to write one test case even when a workflow could go three different ways, so the test could never pass and you had to write the rest by hand. It now writes one case per path.

title: The test result no longer contradicts itself
notes: When a test ran cleanly but couldn't prove the workflow works, the chat used to claim a step had failed — and invent a reason. It now says plainly that nothing broke and which paths still need testing.

title: Atlas no longer promises something it can't check
notes: When a workflow's promise depended on two things at once — say 'urgent AND approved' — Atlas wrote it in a way nothing could ever verify, then rebuilt the workflow over and over trying to satisfy it. It now states the condition in the workflow's own words and moves on.

title: Atlas fills its own blanks instead of asking you twice
notes: When a step was left incomplete, Atlas used to rebuild the whole workflow and then ask you the same question again. It now fills in the obvious answer itself, and questions are written in plain language rather than internal names.

title: Interrupted builds recover instead of being declared lost
notes: If Atlas restarts while you're building, the page now waits it out and tells you your work is safe — instead of giving up after a few seconds and offering to start over.

title: Builds keep running if you close the tab
notes: A build used to live inside one long connection — closing the tab, refreshing, or losing signal took it with you. Builds now run on the server and the page just checks on them, so you can leave and come back.

title: A build in progress survives a restart
notes: Restarting or updating Atlas used to end every build in progress — the next thing you sent came back 'session not found' and the conversation was gone. Builds are now picked back up where they left off.

title: Atlas can add a missing Airtable column
notes: When a workflow needs a column your table doesn't have, Atlas can now offer to add it — instead of rebuilding the workflow to work around it.

title: A problem the builder can't fix is brought to you, not retried
notes: When the builder hits something only you can settle — a column that doesn't exist, a base it can't find — it now asks, instead of rebuilding the whole workflow to try again.

title: Builds stop paying for rebuilds that change nothing
notes: A complex build could rebuild the whole workflow several times over without the workflow changing. It now stops as soon as a rebuild comes back identical — and still says plainly if the self-test never passed.

title: Replies appear in seconds, not minutes
notes: A long reply was typed out one character at a time, and each character redrew the whole screen — so text that had already arrived took minutes to read, and the Build button only appeared at the very end.

title: Builds stop rebuilding when the rebuild changes nothing
notes: A complex workflow could be rebuilt from scratch three extra times without fixing anything — most of a 15-minute build. It now stops as soon as a rebuild comes back with the same problems, and repairs them directly instead.

title: Complex workflows build, and the builder repeats itself less
notes: Workflows with several connected apps could fail to build after minutes of work, blaming your description — they now have room to be written out. The builder also stops re-asking questions you already answered, shows decision rules in plain English, and no longer invents a currency you didn't mention.

title: A custom AI step now uses the input you gave it
notes: A custom AI step was ignoring its configured input and reading the previous step instead. After a routing step that meant it received the routing decision rather than the data, and delivered an error message.

title: Opening a workflow shows that workflow
notes: Opening one workflow after another could show the previous one's diagram and promise under the new one's name. Opening a workflow now replaces everything on screen, and its own diagram is shown.

title: A diagram that can't be right is no longer drawn
notes: If a workflow's steps and its connections don't match, Atlas now says so instead of drawing a tidy diagram of a workflow that doesn't exist.

title: Test an approval step's approve and reject routes
notes: When a test stops at an approval step you can now answer it in the panel, and the run carries on down whichever route you chose — so both halves of an approval workflow get tested.

title: The workflow diagram reads left to right
notes: Workflows with an approval step drew their diagram out of order — the first step low and left, later steps above it. The whole graph is now laid out properly and reads start to finish.

title: Approval workflows can be tested again
notes: Testing a workflow with an approval step no longer hangs — the panel now stops at the approval and says so, instead of spinning forever.

title: Broader workflow shapes & keyboard access
notes: Workflows that chain through a delivery — save a Google Doc, then email its link — now build correctly.
The builder no longer gets stuck rebuilding a workflow that was already valid.
Approval steps and the workflow list are now fully keyboard-operable.

title: Health numbers now count real runs only
notes: Your workflow's success rate and run count now reflect only real runs — test runs from the builder are shown separately instead of being mixed in. A workflow you've tested but that hasn't fired for real now reads "not yet run live" rather than "100% success".
Some success rates will look different (usually lower) after this update. Nothing about your workflows changed — the number is just measuring the right thing now.

title: A clearer, live workflow builder
notes: See a plain-language plan before Atlas builds — approve it in one click.
Watch your workflow assemble step by step, then confirm each step before anything goes live.
Faster, more reliable builds.

title: Atlas builds workflows by talking
notes: Atlas now builds workflows conversationally: it reasons through your request out loud, asks only when it needs a real decision, refuses to wire to a channel that doesn't exist, and tests its own build on real sample data before handing it to you.

title: More reliable builds
notes: The test panel now catches a workflow that delivers broken content, instead of clearing it to go live.
Fixed a case where multi-step email workflows lost the original email; they now build correctly in one pass.
Smoother chat: no more doubled replies, and recurring requests always build a workflow instead of running once.

title: Safer chat actions + a clearer builder
notes: Atlas now shows you a confirmation before it sends an email, posts a message, or writes a record from chat — nothing goes out until you click confirm.
When you describe something recurring or for a whole list, Atlas builds it as a workflow instead of doing it on the spot.
The build view is clearer: one confident summary of what it'll build, and test results no longer linger from a previous workflow.

title: Upload & builder fixes
notes: Larger Knowledge files — like brand kits with images — now upload without errors.
The Feedback button no longer overlaps the test panel's action buttons.

title: A clearer, more reliable builder
notes: The builder now explains what each workflow will deliver in plain language, and tests it against real sample data before you publish.
When a workflow's wiring needs a fix, Atlas repairs it automatically instead of getting stuck.
Test examples are clearly for testing only — they're never part of your published workflow.

title: Test your workflow against its promises
notes: The Run Test panel now checks whether your workflow actually delivered what it promised — for every destination (Atlas inbox, Slack, Gmail, Airtable), and shows the result for each example before you publish.
Fixed: a workflow delivering to somewhere other than Slack could show a false failure in testing even when the delivery succeeded.

title: Build Airtable workflows by clicking, not by pasting IDs
notes: Atlas now reads your Airtable directly: it lists your real bases, reads the real column names, and maps your data onto the columns that actually exist. No more hunting for an opaque base ID. It also refuses to publish a workflow that would write to a column your table doesn't have — previously that record was created with the column silently empty.

title: Multiple destinations now deliver correctly
notes: If a workflow sends its result to more than one place — say Slack and email — every destination now receives the actual content. Previously the second destination could receive a delivery receipt instead of your workflow's output.

title: Send us bugs & feedback in-app
notes: New: a Feedback button (bottom-right on every screen) to report a bug, share an idea, or request a feature — with an auto-captured screenshot, in one click.

title: A fresh sign-in
notes: The sign-in screen has a new look — a glowing Atlas globe and a frosted-glass sign-in panel.

title: Invite your team
notes: Workspace admins can now invite teammates from Account settings — invitees get an email to set their password and join.

title: Atlas is live
notes: Welcome to the Atlas alpha. You'll get a short note like this each time we ship an update.
Request a connector: open Connections and tell us which tools you need — we build what's most in demand.
